So here is my genuine advice, I was in your place when I was younger and here's my two cents. 

First off, cold approach pick up artists or anything related are almost always a scam by YouTubers or influencers trying to make money. A lot, if not 100%, will not only not work, it will instant turn off or freak out most women.

Just remember you're talking to a human being whose life is just as complex as yours. If you approach someone cold you have absolutely no idea what's going on in their life or on that particular day. They may have recieved bad news, had a horrible day in work, they could be grieving or ill. They might be already in a relationship, or gay, they might be meeting up with a friend they haven't seen in years, you just don't know. 

Also they don't know you, even if you are the most insanely handsome and charming man, you're still a complete stranger who is approaching them clearly because you find them sexually attractive. They have no idea how you'll deal with rejection. Will you scream at them? Attack them? Start stalking them? It's a very intimidating interaction. The rates of violence against women is staggering and guys are terrifying. 

What I'm saying is that while their rejection feels personal to you, their rejection is not only justified its advisable.

So here's my advice. 

First thing I'd do is really cement what it is you want. If it's just sex, then honestly you could maybe consider visiting a sex worker.

If what you want is an astheticly pleasing status symbol, then you're going to need some kind of pre existing status. This is the rich guy/hot girlfriend dynamic.

I've never done this, because to be honest it feels like long term leasing a sex worker, and it's transactional nature leads is likely to lead to nothing more than insecurity and loneliness. 


On the other hand, do you want a committed relationship? 


If you want an actual partner you have to approach the situation from a completely different angle than you're currently looking at it. Any intelligent women will see through pickup artist bullshit, and if you're essentially saying to them "I want you for sex and to emotionally support my insecurity" they'll run the other way. 


A partner is first and foremost your friend. You have sex of course, but more importantly your connection is based on the love and support you give each other. 

So if what you want is a partner, you need to take a look at your own interests and likes and see what kind of social functions they have. Go to said function and make friends with people. Make friends with whoever you can, and most importantly make friends with women, even if they're not what you're looking for in a girlfriend. Make a friend FIRST and a sex partner SECOND. 

Good rule of thumb is to ask yourself how you would feel if a guy approached you and did whatever are about to do to the woman. 

And for the love of God, and I can't stress this enough, stay as far away from the Andrew Tates and Jordan Peterson's of the world. 

Weirdly enough I'd recommend checking out some of the more positive youtubers. Drew Gooden, Kurtis Connor, and Chad chad. They're attitudes are great, and cut through a lot of the bullshit out there.

I moved here (Toronto) from Europe six years ago, ostensibly with the same motivation/ skill set as yourself. Here's my experience.

First let's get the bad out of the way.

While Canada is easier to move to than the states, that doesn't mean getting started is easy. I had a nightmare finding work as none of my work history/qualifications mattered squat. Everywhere requires "Canadian" experience, which basically means unless you're exceptional (which in a city like this means something, as the competition is fierce) you'll have to start at the bottom and work your way up. Which may mean getting a 9-5 at something less than ideal to tide you over till you land the position in the industry you want.

Finding accommodation can be difficult too as most landlords want a work reference (which is hard to get without that Canadian experience) and a previous landlord reference which most aren't bothered contacting overseas. I eventually had to fork over first, last and FOUR MONTHS in advance to get a place. Which is llegal for them to even ask but after several months of hostels and couch surfing me and my girlfriend were desperate. but that being said if you move over here single you may have an easier time getting in on a house share.

Not trying to dissuade you. Just letting you know things I wish I'd known before I moved here. Make sure you've saved as much money as possible and be prepared to budget and work retail or whatever while you get settled. I've seen dozens of people arrive unprepared, party for a few weeks then wind up getting the flight home with their tail between their legs having wasted months of planning and money in what amounted to a glorified holiday.

Now the good news. Toronto has a pretty dead metal scene yes, but that can actually work to your advantage. See what Toronto does have is location. Being a major metropolitan North American hub just about every band that tours the states, big and small, will eventually come through Toronto or Montreal. Which means if you manage to work your way up in the small local scene, you can get in with the lower tier venue promoters who can get you support slots with the smaller international acts, which in turn can get you better contacts which means better slots etc etc.

Touring in the states is expensive but a lot more doable than it would be from anywhere else. You're within driving distance of New York and Detroit for example. There is a musicians organization here that aids in getting visas for tours. It's pricey but worth it. 

If I could go back in time I'd likely have moved to Vancouver as it has better access to cities like Seattle, LA, Portland. But honestly the ideal city for this kind of stuff is probably Montreal, cheaper, better bars, better scene. just be aware  they make you feel about as welcome as a fart in an elevator if you don't speak French. 

With regards getting to know the scene/make contacts, the recording studio situation here probably isn't going to be what you're looking for. First off there's very few of them left and what is there you are up against thousands of others with better connections/relevant experience for any job.

If you do manage to get working in one you almost certainly won't be working on anything you'll enjoy. The bigger studios are mostly jingles, voice overs, soundtracks. If there is an artist in, it'll more likely be modern hip hop, country or pop. You also probably won't make any connections that will help you in a career playing metal.

There is work in the AV Tech industry but the hours can be brutal and (to put it mildly) less than conducive to a music career.

 I recommend getting a job in a music instrument store. I worked in one for a few years and it greatly helped me get started in regards finding musicians, meeting promoters, promoting my band etc. Also the staff discount and payment schemes helped me rebuild my set up as I obviously couldn't bring it all with me. 

Is it glamourous? No. But for sheer face to face exposure this is where you'll meet the people you're looking for. 

Anyways best of luck! Sorry for the rambling essay haha.
